§0Orientation

Where this fits

Why a respiratory course opens with skull bones.

The respiratory system is split into two functional halves, and this whole first lecture lives in the upper half plus the framework around it.

Label Key — following air inwards
Nasal / oral cavity
The entry point. Air is drawn in here.
Pharynx
The shared throat passage (behind nose & mouth) — air and food both pass through.
Larynx
The "voice box" — the valve/gateway guarding the airway and producing sound.
Trachea
The "windpipe" — a cartilage-ringed tube heading into the chest.
Carina
The internal ridge where the trachea splits into left & right main bronchi.
Bronchi 1°→3°
Primary (to each lung) → secondary (to each lobe) → tertiary (to each segment), branching finer.

The two halves do different jobs

  • Upper tract (nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx) — a conditioning system. It filters, warms and moistens incoming air so the delicate lungs receive clean, body-temperature, humidified gas.
  • Lower tract (trachea → bronchi → alveoli) — the gas-exchange system, ending in the alveoli where O₂ and CO₂ actually cross into and out of the blood.
Reasoning · why bones first

The upper airway isn't a free-standing tube — it's hollowed out of the skull. The nasal cavity, the air-filled sinuses that drain into it, and the nerves and vessels that supply it all run through specific bones and holes. So you literally cannot explain airflow, a sinus infection, a nosebleed, or why a facial fracture numbs the cheek without the bony map first. That's why Part 1 spends its time on the skull — it's the architecture the respiratory system is built into.

§1LO1 · bones, fossae, foramina for CN I · V · IX · X

The skull, its floor, and four nerves leaving it

Learn the bones, the three stepped "floors" of the skull, and the exact holes four cranial nerves use to escape.

LO1 has three linked parts: (1) name the bones, (2) know the three cranial fossae — the tiered floor the brain rests on — and which bones build each, and (3) know which foramen (hole) each of four nerves passes through: CN I (smell), CN V (face), CN IX and CN X. Parts 2 and 3 connect beautifully: where a nerve sits in the brain decides which fossa — and therefore which hole — it leaves by.

§1.1The bones of the skull

The skull is 22 bones: 8 cranial (the braincase around the brain) and 14 facial (the face and jaws). You don't need to master all 22 equally — but you must be able to name them and, crucially for this block, spot the handful that build the nasal cavity and sinuses.

Label Key — the numbered list (1–6 cranial, 7–14 facial)
1Frontal
Forehead + roof of the orbits + front of the anterior fossa. Single bone.
2Parietal ×2
The paired "walls/roof" of the braincase.
3Temporal ×2
Sides & base; house the ear; form part of the middle & posterior fossae.
4Sphenoid
Central keystone bone — see the note below.
5Occipital
Back & base of skull; contains the foramen magnum.
6Ethmoid
Deep midline bone between the orbits — an MVP for respiration.
7Lacrimal ×2
Tiny bones in the medial orbit; part of the tear-drainage groove.
8Maxilla ×2
Upper jaw; holds upper teeth; forms most of the hard palate & sinus.
9Zygomatic ×2
The cheekbones.
10Inf. nasal concha ×2
The lowest scroll on the lateral nasal wall — its own bone.
11Nasal ×2
The bridge of the nose.
12Palatine ×2
L-shaped bones forming the back of the hard palate & part of the nasal wall.
13Mandible
Lower jaw — the only freely-moving skull bone.
14Vomer
The plough-shaped bone forming the lower nasal septum.
Memory hook · the 8 cranial bones

"PEST Of 6"

Parietal (×2), Ethmoid, Sphenoid, Temporal (×2), Occipital, Frontal — that's 6 types, 8 bones once you double the pairs. For the face, group them as: the 3 midline singles you'll meet again (mandible, vomer, and — cranial — ethmoid) plus 6 paired (maxilla, zygomatic, palatine, nasal, lacrimal, inferior concha).

The two bones that matter most here: ethmoid & sphenoid

Most respiratory anatomy in this lecture hangs off two deep midline bones. Learn these two well and half of LO1–LO3 falls into place.

  • Ethmoid (6) — one small bone doing three jobs: its cribriform plate roofs the nasal cavity (and carries the smell nerve), its perpendicular plate drops down to form the upper nasal septum, and its conchae (scrolls) build the upper lateral wall. It's also air-filled (ethmoid sinuses).
  • Sphenoid (4) — the keystone: it articulates with every other cranial bone, sits centrally in the skull base, forms much of the middle fossa, and is drilled by the three holes the trigeminal nerve's branches use. Remember it and the trigeminal foramina become easy.

Two of those bones already appear when you look at the nasal septum — the midline wall dividing the nose into left and right. It previews §2, but it's worth meeting the bones now:

Label Key
Perpendicular plate of ethmoid
The upper bony part of the septum — a thin blade dropping down from the ethmoid's cribriform plate.
Vomer
The lower & posterior bony septum — the plough-shaped bone sitting on the midline floor.
(anterior, not shown here)
The front of the septum is septal cartilage — flexible, which is why the tip of your nose bends.

So the septum = ethmoid (top) + vomer (bottom-back) + cartilage (front). Keep that three-part picture; you'll reuse it in §2.

§1.2The three cranial fossae

Turn the skull upside down and look inside the base: the floor the brain sits on is not flat. It descends in three tiers, front to back, like a set of shallow stairs — each step cradling a different part of the brain. These are the anterior, middle and posterior cranial fossae.

Label Key — the three tiers (highest → lowest)
Anterior
Highest, most forward step. Cradles the frontal lobes.
Middle
The middle step, "butterfly"-shaped around the centre. Holds the temporal lobes, with the pituitary gland in the central pit (sella turcica).
Posterior
Deepest, most backward step. Holds the cerebellum & brainstem; the foramen magnum opens in its floor.

The learning objective asks specifically which bones build each fossa. The lecture colours the six contributing bones:

Label Key — bones by colour
Frontal
Front of the anterior fossa.
Ethmoid
Central strip of the anterior fossa (the cribriform plate).
Sphenoid
Straddles anterior & middle — the bulk of the middle fossa.
Temporal
Sides of the middle fossa + part of the posterior.
Parietal
Contributes mainly to the walls, a small part of the base.
Occipital
Floor of the posterior fossa.
Which bones build each fossa
FossaBones forming itBrain part it holds
AnteriorFrontal · Ethmoid (cribriform) · lesser wing & body of SphenoidFrontal lobes
MiddleBody & greater wings of Sphenoid · TemporalTemporal lobes + pituitary
PosteriorTemporal (petrous) · OccipitalCerebellum + brainstem
Reasoning · why the tiers matter for nerves

This stepped floor is the key that unlocks the rest of LO1. Each cranial nerve leaves the brain at a particular level, so it exits through a hole in that tier's bone. Smell (CN I) sits at the very front → it leaves through the anterior fossa (ethmoid). The trigeminal (CN V) sits in the middle → its holes are all in the middle fossa (sphenoid). CN IX and X arise from the brainstem at the back → they leave through the posterior fossa (jugular foramen). Fossa → bone → hole. Keep that chain in mind for §1.5–§1.7.

§1.3Foramen vs. fossa vs. paranasal sinus

Your slides pose this directly, and it's genuinely high-yield because the three words describe three different kinds of space in bone. Mixing them up is a classic slip.

Active Anatomy · answered

"What is the difference between a foramen, a fossa and a paranasal sinus?"

Foramen
A hole through bone that something passes through — a nerve or vessel. Plural: foramina. Think doorway.
Fossa
A shallow depression on a bone surface that something sits in — it doesn't go all the way through. Think basin / seat.
Paranasal sinus
An air-filled cavity inside a bone, lined with respiratory mucosa, that drains into the nasal cavity. Think hollow room within the wall.

One-line test: does something pass through it (foramen), rest in it (fossa), or is it a hollow air pocket within the bone (sinus)?

§1.4Cranial nerves — the four you need

There are 12 pairs of cranial nerves. This objective narrows to four, and mostly wants the hole each uses to exit the skull. Meet them on a real specimen first — this is the underside of the brain, looking up at the nerves as they leave:

Label Key — what each looks like
CN I · Olfactory
Not an obvious "nerve" here — it's the olfactory tract/bulb lying in a groove under the frontal lobe (the true nerve filaments are up in the nose).
CN V · Trigeminal
A thick nerve emerging from the side of the pons — the largest cranial nerve.
CN IX · Glossopharyngeal
Fine rootlets from the upper medulla, just above the vagus.
CN X · Vagus
A series of rootlets from the medulla, below IX — leading to the largest, most far-wandering nerve.

Now take them one at a time — each with its function, its foramen, and its bone.

§1.5CN I — Olfactory · smell

Job: smell, and nothing else. Smell receptors sit high in the roof of the nasal cavity; their nerve filaments must travel up into the brain.

Label Key
Cribriform plate
The perforated ("cribriform" = sieve-like) part of the ethmoid bone in the floor of the anterior fossa. Its many tiny holes let the smell filaments through.
ACF / MCF / PCF
Labels for the anterior / middle / posterior cranial fossae — orienting you on the skull base.
Crista galli
The vertical bony ridge sticking up in the midline (an anchor for the brain's covering); sits just in front of the cribriform plate.

The exam fact: CN I passes through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone, into the anterior cranial fossa.

Reasoning · why a sieve?

The receptors are in the nasal roof; the brain is directly above; and the ethmoid roof is the thinnest part of the skull base right there. Rather than one big hole (which would weaken the floor), evolution used a perforated plate — dozens of tiny channels for the ~20 bundled filaments, keeping the bone strong. Function (smell must reach the brain) explains the form (a sieve).

Memory hook · three "olfactory" things aren't the same

Examiners love this trap. The olfactory nerve = the filaments in the nose passing through the cribriform plate. The olfactory bulb = the swelling that sits on top of the plate (inside the skull) receiving them. The olfactory tract = the stalk carrying the signal back toward the brain. Nerve = below the plate; bulb & tract = above it (they're actually brain tissue).

Clinical · anosmia & CSF leak

Because the cribriform plate is thin and the filaments cross it, a hard blow to the head can shear the filaments → loss of smell (anosmia). A fracture through the plate can also tear the brain's lining, letting cerebrospinal fluid drip from the nose (CSF rhinorrhoea) — a clear watery nasal discharge after head trauma is a red flag.

§1.6CN V — Trigeminal · face sensation (+ chewing)

The trigeminal is the great sensory nerve of the face (touch, pain, temperature) and also drives the muscles of chewing. Its name is the mnemonic: tri-gemini = "three twins" → it has three divisions.

Label Key — the three divisions (top of face → bottom)
V₁ Ophthalmic
Sensation to the forehead, upper eyelid, bridge of nose & eye.
V₂ Maxillary
Sensation to the mid-face, cheek, upper lip, upper teeth & nasal cavity.
V₃ Mandibular
Sensation to the lower face, jaw, lower teeth & front of tongue, plus motor to the chewing muscles.

Here's the centrepiece exam fact: the three divisions leave through three different holes, all in the sphenoid, all in the middle fossa. Front-to-back on the sphenoid, top-to-bottom on the face:

The trigeminal exits — must-know
DivisionForamen (hole)BoneHeads toward…
V₁ OphthalmicSuperior orbital fissureSphenoidthe orbit (eye)
V₂ MaxillaryForamen rotundumSphenoidpterygopalatine fossa → mid-face
V₃ MandibularForamen ovaleSphenoidinfratemporal fossa → jaw
Memory hook · V1 · V2 · V3 exits

"Standing Room Only"

Superior orbital fissure · Rotundum · Ovale — in order for V₁, V₂, V₃. And the numbering follows the face top-down (V₁ forehead → V₃ jaw), while the holes run roughly front-to-back across the sphenoid. Rotundum = "round", ovale = "oval" — the names describe the hole shapes.

Reasoning · why three separate exits?

Behind the eye, the trigeminal fans out from a single ganglion into three territories — orbit, mid-face, jaw — that head to three different regions of the face. Each needs its own exit pointed toward its target, so the sphenoid carries three holes rather than one. The fissure for V₁ opens into the orbit (where the eye is); rotundum aims at the mid-face; ovale drops toward the jaw.

Clinical · where you'll meet V

Trigeminal neuralgia — sudden electric-shock facial pain confined to one division's territory. Dental anaesthesia — dentists block branches of V₂ (upper teeth) and V₃ (lower teeth). Shingles in V₁ threatens the eye, because V₁ supplies the cornea. Knowing the territories tells you exactly where a lesion of each division will numb.

§1.7CN IX & CN X — Glossopharyngeal & Vagus

These two (together with CN XI) arise close together from the brainstem at the back of the skull, so they share the same posterior-fossa exit: the jugular foramen, between the temporal and occipital bones.

Label Key
Glossopharyngeal (IX)
Glosso = tongue, pharyngeal = throat. Sensation to the posterior ⅓ of the tongue & pharynx, taste there, the gag reflex (sensory limb), and BP/O₂ sensing at the carotid.
Jugular foramen
The large hole between the temporal & occipital bones in the posterior fossa. Named because the internal jugular vein also leaves here.
Label Key
Vagus (X)
Vagus = "wandering". The great parasympathetic nerve — supplies the larynx & pharynx (voice, swallowing) then wanders down to the heart, lungs and gut.
Jugular foramen
The vagus's exit — the same hole as CN IX (and XI).
Foramen magnum
The large central hole in the occipital bone where the brainstem becomes the spinal cord; the vertebral arteries and CN XI's spinal root pass here. (The vagus proper uses the jugular foramen — the magnum is labelled for orientation.)
Reasoning · why IX, X (and XI) share one hole

They spring from the medulla within millimetres of each other at the back of the brainstem, and all head for the neck. The nearest large exit in the posterior fossa is the jugular foramen, which is already there to drain the big venous sinus — so all three nerves use it. Proximity in the brain → shared exit.

Clinical · jugular foramen syndrome

Because IX, X and XI travel together, a single mass at the jugular foramen (e.g. a tumour) can knock out all three at once — trouble swallowing and a diminished gag (IX/X), a hoarse voice (X), and a weak shoulder shrug (XI). One location, three nerves, a recognisable cluster of signs.

LO1 master table — the four nerves & their exits
NerveDoesForamenBoneFossa
I OlfactorySmellCribriform plateEthmoidAnterior
V₁ OphthalmicSensation: forehead/eyeSup. orbital fissureSphenoidMiddle
V₂ MaxillarySensation: mid-faceForamen rotundumSphenoidMiddle
V₃ MandibularSensation: jaw + chewingForamen ovaleSphenoidMiddle

§1.R Recall checklist — LO1 essentials
  • 22 bones = 8 cranial (PEST Of 6) + 14 facial. Respiratory MVPs: ethmoid & sphenoid.
  • Ethmoid does 3 jobs: cribriform plate (roof) · perpendicular plate (septum) · conchae (lateral wall). Sphenoid = keystone + trigeminal holes.
  • Nasal septum = perpendicular plate of ethmoid (top) + vomer (bottom) + septal cartilage (front).
  • Three fossae: Anterior (frontal · ethmoid · sphenoid) → Middle (sphenoid · temporal) → Posterior (temporal · occipital).
  • Foramen = through · Fossa = sit in · Sinus = air cavity within bone.
  • CN I → cribriform plate (ethmoid). Nerve ≠ bulb ≠ tract.
  • CN V "Standing Room Only": V₁ SOF · V₂ rotundum · V₃ ovale — all sphenoid.
  • CN IX & X → jugular foramen (temporal/occipital), posterior fossa. IX/X/XI together = jugular foramen syndrome.
